to oxygenates and from C1 to C3.[4,5] Compared with those liquid-phase CO2RR products which usually undergo low Faradaic efficiencies and require energy-intensive downstream separation,[6,7] gaseous CO is a highly desirable alternative because of its spontaneous separation and purification for further use as feedstock of valuable fuel and chemical synthesis through existing chemical technologies.[2–4,8–10] In low-cost aqueous electrolytes, electroreduction reaction of CO2 to CO takes place on solid–liquid–gaseous interface of electrode materials via a relatively simple two-electron transfer process,[2–4] that is, CO2 +  2H+ +  2e− → CO + H2O, but with the efficiency relying on the heterogeneous electrocatalysis,[2,5,11] which is associated with indispensable mass transport of CO2 and its derivative ions/molecules toward electroactive sites, electron transfer from conductive support to electroactive sites, and reduction reactions at electroactive sites.[11] To satisfy the multifunctional
requirements, it needs judicious engineering of electrocatalytic materials in both electroactive site and electrode structure levels to have abundant electroactive sites with high intrinsic activity, sufficient accessibility of electroactive sites, and high capability of simultaneous electron transfer and mass transport for achieving high current densities at low overpotentials.[2,5,11,12] Precious metals, typically Au- and Ag-based nanomaterials,[13–17] are the most active electrocatalysts for the CO product of CO2RR with the Faradaic efficiency of >90%. However, the scarcity and high cost essentially limit their practical application in CO2 electrolyzers. With an aim to replace Au- and Ag-based highcost materials, considerable research efforts have been focused on developing various electrocatalysts based on earth-abundant elements. These include monometallic Cu atomic nanosheets[18] and pairs,[19] Sn nanoparticles,[20] Zn nanosheets,[21,22] bimetallic alloys of Cu with Al,[23] In[24] and Sn,[25–28] metal oxides,[29,30] and chalcogenides,[31,32] as well as single-atom Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni carbonitrides[33–38] and organometallic complexes.[39,40] Nevertheless, most of them still require high overpotentials to deliver desirable current densities due to their modest activity toward the reduction of chemically inert CO2 molecule. Whereas these low-dimensional nanocatalysts can provide abundant electroactive sites, they have to be immobilized on planar current collectors by making use of insulative polymer binders for large-scale
Designing highly selective and cost-effective electrocatalysts toward electrochemical carbon dioxide (CO2) reduction is crucial for desirable transformation of greenhouse gas into fuels or high-value chemical products. Here, the authors report intermetallic Cu3Sn that is in situ formed and seamlessly integrated on self-supported bimodal nanoporous Cu skeleton (Cu3Sn/Cu) via a spontaneous alloying of Sn and Cu as robust electrocatalyst for selective electroreduction of CO2 to CO. By virtue of Sn atoms strengthening CO adsorption on Cu atoms, the intermetallic Cu3Sn has an intrinsic activity of ≈10.58 μA cm−2, more than 80-fold higher than that of monometallic Cu. By virtue of hierarchical bicontinuous nanoporous Cu architecture facilitating electron transfer and CO2 and proton mass transport and offering high specific surface areas for full use of electroactive Cu3Sn sites, the nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu hybrid electrodes produce CO at a low overpotential of 0.09 V, and exhibit high partial current density of ≈15 mA cm−2geo at overpotential of 0.59 V, along with excellent stability and selectivity of 91.5% Faradaic efficiency. The outstanding electrochemical performance make them attractive alternatives to precious Au- and Ag-based electrocatalysts for building lowcost CO2 electrolyzers to selectively produce CO.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide (CO2) powered by electricity from renewable and plentiful solar and wind resources provides an attractive approach to transformation of greenhouse gas into carbon-based fuels and chemicals, promising a sustainable scenario of carbon-neutral energy cycle.[1–3] Owing to the multiproton and multielectron processes, CO2 electroreduction reaction (CO2RR) mediated by catalysts usually gives rise to a variety of products, ranging from hydrocarbons

practical use.[18–22,24–41] This is neither cost-effective nor efficient because it inevitably leads to high contact resistance at supplementary abundant interfaces and dense stack of electroactive blocks, which substantially hinder electron transfer, mass diffusion, and electroactive site accessibility, respectively.[42–46]
Here, we report that self-supported nanoporous Cu–Sn hybrid electrodes composed of hexagonal Cu3Sn intermetallic compound hold genuine potential as robust and cost-effective electrocatalysts for highly selective electroreduction of CO2 to CO in aqueous KHCO3 electrolyte. Therein, the electroactive Cu3Sn is in situ formed and seamlessly integrated on the surface of hierarchical nanoporous Cu skeleton (Cu3Sn/Cu) via a spontaneous alloying of Sn and Cu in a chemical dealloying process. Owing to the incorporation of Sn strengthening the CO adsorption of Cu, the constituent Cu3Sn shows exceptionally selective CO2RR for the CO product, with an intrinsic activity of ≈10.58 μA cm−2 that is more than 80-fold higher than that of monometallic Cu (≈0.13 μA cm−2). As a consequence of hierarchical bicontinuous nanoporous Cu architecture facilitating electron transfer/mass transport and simultaneously enabling sufficient accessibility of electroactive Cu3Sn sites, the nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu hybrid electrodes exhibit high partial current density of ≈15 mA cm−2geo and selectivity of 91.5% Faradaic efficiency for CO at overpotential of 0.59  V, along with excellent stability. The outstanding electrochemical performance makes them attractive alternatives to precious Auand Ag-based cathode electrocatalysts for potential use in CO2 electrolyzers.

sections.heading: 2.1. Preparation and Structures of Intermetallic Electrocatalysts
sections.text:
Monolithic nanoporous Cu–Sn hybrid electrodes are fabricated by a facile and scalable alloying/dealloying approach,[44,47–50] with both chemical components and nanoporous microstructures to be regulated by their quasi-eutecticstructured precursor alloys of Cu20−xSnxAl80 (x  =  0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5  at%) (Figure S1, Supporting Information),[50] which are conveniently produced by arc-melting pure Cu and Al metals with/without addition of Sn metal. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of Cu20−xSnxAl80 alloys demonstrate that they are primarily composed of α-Al and intermetallic Al2Cu phases, in addition to metallic Sn phase (Figure S2, Supporting Information). As illustrated in representative scanning electron microscope energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDS) elemental mapping images of Cu20−xSnxAl80 (x  =  2), these precursor alloys present in a quasi-eutectic structure consist of alternating ≈500-nm-thick α-Al and Al2Cu lamellas,[51] in which the Sn element uniformly distributes (Figure S3, Supporting Information). When chemically dealloyed in N2-purged KOH aqueous solution at 90  °C, such unique multiphase nanostructure enables a hierarchical nanoporous architecture through a successively selective etching process of less-noble Al component from α-Al and Al2Cu lamellas. While for the free Sn species, it thermodynamically prefers alloying with low-coordination surface Cu atoms to form hexagonal intermetallic Cu3Sn and/or monoclinic intermetallic
Cu6Sn5 on nanoscaled Cu ligaments, depending on the Sn content in the precursor alloys.[52]
Figure 1a shows a typical SEM image of nanoporous Cu–Sn hybrid electrode, which is fabricated by chemically dealloying Cu20−xSnxAl80 (x  =  2). It displays a hierarchical nanoporous structure consisting of ≈220-nm large channels and nanoporous Cu lamellas with ≈27-nm small nanopores (Figure 1b), due to the fast dissolution of α-Al lamellas and selective etching of Al from Al2Cu lamellas, respectively.[49,50] Compared with a bimodal and uniform nanoporous structure of nanoporous bare Cu from precursor Cu20Al80 alloy (Figure S4a, Supporting Information), the nanoporous Cu–Sn hybrid electrode does not show any obvious structure change except for some coarsening regions on the nanoporous Cu lamellas (Figure 1a), which probably result from the incorporation of Sn essentially depressing the surface diffusion of Cu and Sn atoms via the Cu–Sn covalent bonds. Figure  1c presents XRD patterns of nanoporous Cu–Sn hybrid electrode from Cu20−xSnxAl80 (x  =  2) precursor alloy. There appear neoformative diffraction peaks at 2ϴ = 37.8°, 41.8°, 43.3°, 57.3°, 77.5° corresponding to (200), (002), (201), (202), and (203) planes of the hexagonal Cu3Sn (Figure 1c), in addition to four characteristic peaks at 2ϴ = 43.3°, 50.4°, 74.1°, 89.8° attributed to the (111), (200), (220), and (311) reflections of Cu (JCPDS 04-0836).[52] X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) survey (Figure S5, Supporting Information) and EDS spectrum (Figure S6, Supporting Information) confirm the presence of Sn, in addition to Cu and a bit of residual internal Al. The Sn distributes along the nanoporous Cu lamellas, as revealed by representative SEM-EDS elemental mapping images of asdealloyed nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu hybrid electrode (Figure  1d). Figure 1e shows a high-resolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM) image of Cu3Sn/Cu interface, where both two different phases are identified by their corresponding fast Fourier transform (FFT) patterns (insets of Figure  1e). Whereas they are in different crystallographic structures, the intermetallic Cu3Sn still grows epitaxially on the face-centered cubic Cu ligaments only with obvious strains in initial atomic layers. These observations indicate the presence of intermetallic Cu3Sn on formation of monolithic nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu hybrid electrode during the chemical dealloying process of Cu20−xSnxAl80 (x  =  2). Such unique nanoporous architecture not only facilitates electron transfer and mass transport but also enables exceptional stability, in sharp contrast with those electrodes made of low-dimensional nanostructures, which are in weakly physical contact. As the Sn content in the Cu20−xSnxAl80 precursor alloy increases, there additionally forms intermetallic Cu6Sn5 in their corresponding nanoporous Cu–Sn hybrid electrodes via the transformation of Cu3Sn to Cu6Sn5 (Figure S7, Supporting Information).[52] This is attested by the observation that the characteristic peaks of monoclinic Cu6Sn5 in their XRD patterns gradually intensify while the Cu3Sn ones attenuate (Figure  1c and Figure S8, Supporting Information). When x  =  5, the nanoporous Cu–Sn hybrid electrode is dominantly composed of intermetallic Cu6Sn5 that is integrated on nanoporous Cu lamellas, that is, nanoporous Cu6Sn5/Cu (Figure 1c and Figure S9, Supporting Information).
Ex situ Cu 2p and Sn 3d XPS spectra of nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu and Cu6Sn5/Cu hybrid electrodes are shown in Figures  2a, and  2c, respectively. In addition to their metallic states that

correspond to the internal Cu and Sn atoms in both Cu ligaments and intermetallic Cu3Sn or Cu6Sn5, the surface Cu and Sn atoms are in Cu+ and Sn4+ states, respectively, due to unavoidable oxidation in air.[26,53] Considering that the Cu+ has a binding energy very similar to the metal state of Cu, the X-ray generated Auger spectra are collected in the Cu L3M45M45 region to verify the presence of Cu+. As shown in Figure 2b, there presents a characteristic peak of Cu+ at 916.3 eV, in addition to the primary one (918.7  eV) assigned to the metallic state of Cu.[25,53] Nevertheless, the Pourbaix diagrams of Sn and Cu thermodynamically suggest their oxidized surface atoms can be reduced to metallic states at the highly negative potentials.[54] Density functional theory (DFT) calculations based on the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) functional demonstrate that the d-band of Cu in intermetallic Cu3Sn exhibits a sharper peak in the energy range from −4.5 to −1.0 eV due to electron localization, which implies the formation of Cu–Sn covalent bonds (Figure 2d). This gives rise to the up-shift of the d-band of Cu in intermetallic Cu3Sn, strengthening the adsorption energy of CO. To verify this expectation, the CO adsorption behaviors on Cu3Sn(2110) surface are investigated by DFT calculations. As shown in Figure S10, Supporting Information, there are two possible CO adsorption configurations, that is, the Cu top sites and the Cu–Cu bridge sites, with the adsorption energies of −1.24 and −1.40 eV, respectively, due to the incorporation of Sn breaking the pure Cu surface. In contrast, the adsorption energies of CO on the top, bridge, and hollow sites of Cu(111) surface are −1.05, −1.18, and −1.22 eV (Figure S11, Supporting Information).

sections.heading: 2.2. Electrochemical Characterization of Intermetallic Electrocatalysts
sections.text:
To assess the electrocatalytic properties, self-supported nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu, Cu6Sn5/Cu, and bare Cu electrodes are directly used as the working electrodes in an H-cell for electrochemical measurements (Figure S12, Supporting Information), with the Ag/AgCl electrode and the Pt foil as the reference electrode and the counter electrode, respectively. Figure 3a shows representative linear scanning voltammetry curves of nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu, Cu6Sn5/Cu, and bare Cu electrodes in N2 or CO2 saturated 0.1 m KHCO3 electrolyte, where the potential is iR-corrected and calibrated with respect to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), and the current density (Jgeo) is normalized by geometry area. In N2-saturated 0.1 m KHCO3 electrolyte, the nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu electrode exhibits much lower current density than the nanoporous Cu. This observation indicates the inferior activities of intermetallic Cu3Sn and Cu6Sn5 toward the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) due to the incorporation of Sn. While in CO2 saturated 0.1  m KHCO3 electrolyte, the current density of nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu increases remarkably to ≈20 mA cm−2 from the value of ≈5 mA cm−2 in N2-saturated 0.1 m KHCO3 electrolyte at overpotential of 0.59 V, in sharp contrast to those of nanoporous Cu and Cu6Sn5/Cu. To further pinpoint their reduction products, electrolyses are performed at given potentials to periodically quantify the gas products by gas chromatography and the liquid products by 1 H nuclear magnetic resonance (H-NMR) spectroscopy. When mediated by the nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu electrode, the CO and H2 are the dominant products, with negligible liquid-phase HCOOH (Figure S13a, Supporting Information). Figure 3b compares the Faradaic efficiencies of CO and H2 for all three nanoporous electrodes, demonstrating that nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu exhibits superior selective electrocatalysis of CO2RR, with the Faradaic efficiency values higher than 80% between −0.65 and −0.8  V versus RHE for the CO product. The maximum Faradaic efficiency of CO reaches ≈91.5% at overpotential of 0.59 V, enlisting the nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu to have the partial current density of CO (JCO) of 15 mA cm−2 (Figure 3c). This is in sharp contrast with the nanoporous Cu and Cu6Sn5/Cu, by which their products are mainly H2 in addition to some liquid products such as HCOOH and C2H5OH (Figures S13b,c and S14, Supporting Information). As shown in Figure 3c, the nanoporous Cu and Cu6Sn5/Cu electrodes only exhibit the JCO of ≈0.35 and ≈0.38  mA  cm−2 at overpotential of 0.59  V, respectively. When the potential decreases to −0.8 V versus RHE, the JCO of nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu is as high as 30 mA cm−2. The superior electrocatalytic activity of nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu is also manifested by the lowest Tafel slope of ≈117 mV dec−1 (Figure 3d and Figure S15, Supporting Information). These facts demonstrate the intermetallic Cu3Sn to work as electroactive sites for the selective electroreduction of CO2 to CO, with the rate-limited step of the formation of CO2*− intermediate species on the Cu3Sn surface.[15,54,55] To evaluate the intrinsic activity of Cu3Sn, Cu6Sn5, and Cu, electrochemical surface areas (ECSAs) of nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu, Cu6Sn5/Cu, and Cu electrodes are estimated by a double-layer capacitance (Cdl) approach, in which cyclic voltammetry is performed in a non-Faradaic voltage window (Figure S16, Supporting Information).[26,55] Based on their linear slopes in the

With a premise of metallic Cu part in nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu electrode having the same ECSACu/mCu ratio as the bare nanoporous Cu, the ECSACu,Cu3Sn/Cu is estimated in terms of the equation, ECSACu,Cu3Sn/Cu  =  mCu,Cu3Sn/CuECSACu/mCu. Here, mCu,Cu3Sn/Cu is the mass of Cu part in the nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu electrode, and mCu and ECSACu are the mass and the ECSA value of nanoporous Cu electrode. As a result, ECSACu3Sn,Cu3Sn/Cu  =  ECSACu3Sn/Cu  − mCu,Cu3Sn/CuECSACu/mCu. The intrinsic activity of Cu3Sn is further calculated to be ≈10.58 μA cm−2, more than 80- and 30-fold higher than those of Cu (0.13  μA  cm−2) and Cu6Sn5 (0.31  μA  cm−2) (Figure  3d). In view that those nanoporous Cu–Sn alloy electrodes have different ratios of more electroactive Cu3Sn and less electroactive Cu6Sn5 according to their distinct diffraction intensities (Table S1, Supporting Information), their Faradaic efficiencies and JCO values at overpotential of 0.59 V strongly depend on the Sn content (Figure  3e), and reach the maximum values at the Sn of 10  at%, that is, the nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu electrode prepared from precursor Cu20−xSnxAl80 (x = 2) alloy. These electrochemical parameters enlist nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu to outperform most of state-of-the-art nonprecious metal-based CO2RR electrocatalysts in CO2 saturated 0.1  m  KHCO3 electrolyte for the CO product (Figure 3f and Table S2, Supporting Information).
To elucidate the origin of superior CO2RR activity of Cu3Sn, DFT calculations are conducted on the basis of thermodynamically stable Cu3Sn(2110). Therein, the CO2* thermodynamically prefers to be adsorbed on two Cu atoms via the CuO and CuC bonds during the optimization process (Figure S18, Supporting Information). Figure 4 shows the free energy diagram for the most favorable pathways of CO2 reduction to CO,
H2, and HCOOH products at 0 V versus RHE. Because of electron transfer from Sn to Cu, the CO2 prefers to be adsorbed on surface negatively charged Cu atoms of Cu3Sn(2110) to form *COO intermediate species, where there involves one electron transfer. With the hydrogenation, the H* can initially adsorb on the CuCu bridge sites nearby the *COO Cu atoms. Even though the H* protons close to C atoms have a free energy of −0.19 eV (initial state 1, IS1), it takes 0.2 eV to generate H2 via a HER, and 0.09 eV to form HCOO* for the further production of HCOOH with energy barrier of as high as 0.34 eV. In contrast, the H* close to the O atoms (IS2) only needs to overcome the energy barrier of 0.0056 eV for the formation of *COOH. Next, there spontaneously takes place another proton-coupled electron transfer to liberate H2O, leaving bound *CO. Finally, this bound *CO desorbs in a chemical step to form the gaseous CO product. This reaction pathway is consistent with experimental measurement with the Tafel slope of 117  mV  dec−1, which implies the rate-limited step of one electron transfer to CO2 molecule.[2–4,15,54,55] In contrast, there forms the HCOO* intermediate on Cu6Sn5(221) with the reaction energy of −1.38 eV (Figure S19, Supporting Information), which leads to HCOOH product with a high reaction energy of 0.67 eV.
Electrochemical durability of nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu electrode is performed at −0.7 V versus RHE in CO2 saturated 0.1 m KHCO3 electrolyte for 120 h, during which the fresh electrolyte is used after every 24-h measurement. As shown in Figure 5a, the current density does not change evidently, along with the Faraday efficiency of CO remaining >80%. In the tested electrolyte, there is not evident increase in Cu and Sn ion concentrations according to inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) analysis. These observations indicate the excellent chemical and structural stability of nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu electrode because of the steady nanoporous architecture, in which the electroactive Cu3Sn sites are seamlessly integrated on the Cu skeleton via an in situ alloying method. As demonstrated by XPS analysis of both Cu 2p and Sn 3d (Figure  5b,c), the chemical states of Cu and Sn elements in nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu does not evidently change. Moreover, the nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu electrode still maintains the same morphology and crystallographic structure after a long-term durability measurement (Figure 5d and Figure S20, Supporting Information).

sections.heading: 3. Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, we have developed a facile and scalable dealloying approach that is associated with an in situ and spontaneous alloying of Sn and Cu to fabricate monolithic nanoporous intermetallic compound/metal hybrid electrodes for electrochemical reduction of CO2. There in situ forms hexagonal Cu3Sn and/ or monoclinic Cu6Sn5 intermetallic compounds on hierarchical nanoporous Cu skeleton, depending on the Sn content in precursor alloys. Because of the incorporation of Sn strengthening the CO adsorption of Cu atoms to a proper value, the intermetallic Cu3Sn works as electroactive site with an intrinsic activity of as high as ≈10.58  μA  cm−2, which is more than 30- and 80-fold higher than those of Cu6Sn5 and monometallic Cu. By virtue of bimodal nanoporous architecture to facilitate electron

Along with excellent stability, the nanoporous Cu3Sn/Cu hybrid electrode holds genuine potential as attractive alternatives to precious Au- and Ag-based electrocatalysts for building low-cost CO2 electrolyzers to selectively produce CO.

sections.heading: 4. Experimental Section
sections.text:
Fabrication of Nanoporous Cu–Sn Hybrid Electrodes: All nanoporous Cu–Sn hybrid electrodes were prepared by a facile and scalable alloying/ dealloying procedure. Precursor alloy ingots of Cu20−xSnxAl80 (x  =  0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5  at%) were first produced by arc-melting Cu (99.9%) and Al (99.9%) with/without the addition of Sn (99.9%) in Ar atmosphere. These precursor alloys were cut into thin sheets and sanded to thickness of ≈400  μm. The as-prepared alloy sheets were chemically dealloyed to develop nanoporous Cu and Cu–Sn alloy hybrid electrocatalysts in a N2-purged 6  m  KOH aqueous solution at 90  °C for 4  h. These nanoporous catalysts were rinsed in pure water (18.2 MΩ cm) to remove chemical substance in nanopore channels and used for electrochemical measurements and microstructure characterizations.
Structural Characterization: The microstructural features and element distributions of all nanoporous Cu–Sn electrocatalysts were
characterized using a field-emission SEM (JEOL JSM-6700F, 15  keV) equipped with an X-ray EDS. The interfacial structure of multiphase nanoporous Cu–Sn electrodes was observed by a field-emission transmission electron microscope (JEOL JEM-2100F, 200  keV). XRD measurements were conducted on a D/max 2500pc diffractometer using Cu Kα radiation. XPS analysis was carried out on a Thermo ESCALAB 250Xi with an Al anode. Charging effects were compensated by shifting binding energies based on the adventitious C 1s peak (284.8  eV). The compositions were analyzed by ICP-OES (Thermo electron). NMR spectra were recorded on Bruker NMR spectrometers (AVANCE-III HD 500). Gas components analysis was performed on gas chromatograph (SHIMADZU GC-2014) with thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and flame ionization detector (FID).
Electrochemical Measurements: All electrochemical experiments were carried out on a classic three-electrode setup in an H-cell, with a platinum foil and a Ag/AgCl electrode as the counter electrode and the reference electrode, respectively, and nanoporous Cu or Cu–Sn electrodes were directly employed as the working electrodes. The CO2RR electrocatalytic measurements were conducted in CO2-saturated aqueous electrolyte of 0.1  m  KHCO3 at ambient temperature, wherein N2 or CO2 gas flow was kept at the rate of 40  mL  min−1, respectively. Chronoamperometry was performed at −0.7 V to evaluate the durability of electrocatalysts. All the potentials were calibrated with respect to RHE and iR-corrected according to the equations, E  =  EAg/AgCl  +  0.5964  V and E  =  EAg/AgCl  −  iR  +  0.5964  V, respectively. Their electrochemical impedance spectroscopy was collected at the overpotential of 0.1  V in a frequency range from 100  kHz to 10 mHz in 0.1  m  KHCO3 aqueous electrolyte.
Carbon Dioxide Reduction Product Analysis: To quantify the gas products during electrolysis, CO2 gas (Airgas, 99.995%) was delivered into the cathodic compartment at a rate of 40  mL  min−1 and vented

into a gas chromatoraph (Shimadzu GC-2014) equipped with a TCD and a FID. Therein, the TCD was used to detect H2 while the FID was employed for the quantitative analysis of CO content and/or any other alkane species. The gas concentrations were determined by an external standard method. Briefly, the standard samples of gases with given concentrations (C0) were first measured at the same chromatographic conditions as the gas products to be tested. Their standard curves were established by making use of the corresponding linear relationships between the origin of coordinate and their integral areas of characteristic peaks (A0), which correspond to the concentration C  =  0 and C0, respectively. When measuring the gas product with an integral area of characteristic peak (Ai), its concentration (Ci) could be determined by their corresponding standard curves and equation, that is, Ci  =  AiC0/A0. The Faradaic efficiency was calculated according to FE = (nFN/Q) × 100%, where n was the number of electron transferred in the Faradaic process, F = 96 485 C mol−1 was the Faradaic constant, N was the amount of the generated product in this process, and Q was the total charge passed through the whole reaction. 1H NMR spectroscopy (Bruker AVANCE-III HD 500) was employed at the end of experiments to test for possible production of liquid products, in which 0.5  mL electrolyte was mixed with 0.1 mL D2O and 0.05 μL dimethyl sulfoxide (Sigma, 99.9%) was added as an internal standard.
Computational Methods: In this work, DFT calculations were carried out using the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP) code with the version of 5.4.4. The pseudopotentials were generated with the consideration of the valence state 4s13d10 for Cu, 5s24d105p2 for Sn, 2s22p2 for C, 2s22p4 for O, and 1s1 for H by the scalar relativistic all-electron Blöchl’s projector augmented-wave method. The cutoff of the plane wave was set to 400  eV. The Brillouin zone was sampled with 3 × 4 × 1 Monkhorst-Pack K-point mesh. The exchange correlation potential was described by the GGA with PBE functional. According to the HRTEM image in Figure  1b, the Cu3Sn(2 110) was considered as the surface of the catalyst. Therefore, the slab of Cu3Sn(2 110) with eight-layer atoms was used as the calculation model in DFT calculations. The bottom three-layer atoms of the slab were fixed and the top five-layer atoms were fully relaxed. To prevent artificial interaction effects, the vacuum distance between adjacent slabs was set to 20  Å. The Gaussian smearing of 0.05  eV was used to accelerate the convergence of the electronic structure. The tolerable residual force and energy errors were set to 0.02 eV Å−1 and 10−4  eV, respectively. A continuum solvent model provided by VASPsol was used to accurately consider the interactions between the adsorbate and the solvent.
